title: The House Money Effect (Why We Gamble With Found Money)
description: People treat money differently based on its source. Unexpected windfalls—gambling winnings, gifts, tax refunds—are spent more recklessly than earned money, because they feel like “house money,” not real wealth.
shortDescription: People treat money differently based on its source. Unexpected windfalls—gambling winnings, gifts, tax refunds—are spent more recklessly than earned money, because they feel like “house money,” not real wealth.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: People treat money differently based on its source. Unexpected windfalls—gambling winnings, gifts, tax refunds—are spent more recklessly than earned money, because they feel like “house money,” not real wealth.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: At a casino, after winning $200, you start placing riskier bets because “it’s the casino’s money anyway.”
A tax refund goes straight to a luxury purchase, while the same amount from salary would have been saved.
A bonus is treated as “fun money,” while base salary is budgeted carefully.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Taking more risk with gains than with initial capital.
Gambling until all “house money” is lost, then feeling less bad than if it were savings.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I’m playing with the casino’s money now.”
“It’s a bonus, so I’m treating myself.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Your spending spikes after a windfall, with little to show for it later.
You’re taking risks with gains that you’d never take with your original savings.
A lottery win or inheritance disappears within a few years.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Thaler and Johnson (1990) showed that prior outcomes affect risk‑taking. Gains are mentally separated from “own” money, so losses feel less painful. The brain tags windfalls as less serious, lowering the guardrails.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Immediately transfer windfalls into a savings or investment account before you mentally label it as “fun.”
Ask: “If this money had come from my regular paycheck, what would I do with it?”
Set a rule: spend 10–20% on fun, save the rest. The framing acknowledges the joy without letting it dominate.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking that enjoying windfall money is inherently wrong; a little celebration is fine. The error is when the entire sum evaporates without trace.
Forgetting that all money is fungible. A dollar from a lottery is the same as a dollar from labor.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A woman wins $5,000 in a raffle. She books a luxury vacation instead of paying off a high‑interest credit card. The vacation is wonderful, but she returns to debt that costs her more in interest than the trip was worth. The house money blinded her to the real cost of her existing obligations.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Money doesn’t know where it came from. Spend it all like it was earned through sweat, and you’ll still have it when the wind stops blowing.
